prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and market power in differentiated-product markets with endogenous prices, which transformed empirical industrial organisation and the analysis of competition, mergers and welfare

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed from B050 (Melitz, Helpman) to B001 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn). The change rests on two things in the exchange, not on the support count. First, I conceded in round 1 that B050's credit is partly outside the ballot entry (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum, and Redding as a later contributor). Hassler and Andersson pressed the same point, and I think it weighs more than I first allowed. Second, B001's unit of prize can be defined tightly. The method-level citation is estimating demand and market power with endogenous prices in differentiated-product markets. That is a measurement advance with a named, jointly authored core (Berry 1994 and BLP 1995). It has about three decades of use in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and it has spread into trade, productivity and markup measurement. As a macroeconomist who works with firm-level microdata, I see this spread directly. Markup and misallocation questions in my own field depend on the demand-side and production-function tools that this tradition made routine. The method changed what can be measured about substitution, markups and welfare, so I treat it as a discovery-enabling measurement contribution, not merely a toolkit. Maturity is not contested by anyone. I would still say B050 is the conceptually richer idea, because selection and reallocation across heterogeneous firms is a general mechanism. But on the common criteria of originality, durability, breadth and clean credit, B001 now looks to me at least as strong, and cleaner on attribution.
statement.case_against: The main reservations are the ones the chair has already listed. The first is toolkit versus discovery, and some members will weigh a method below a substantive finding. The second is the third slot: Levinsohn rather than Bresnahan leaves out the founder of the new empirical IO programme, and a three-name cap also leaves out Reiss, Benkard and Levin. The third is that Pakes's dynamic-games and production-function work is only partly covered by a demand-focused citation. Applied BLP estimates are known to be sensitive to numerical implementation, instruments and functional form. From my distance I cannot judge how far these sensitivities change real merger conclusions. I am also an outsider to industrial organisation, so my assessment depends on colleagues' accounts and on background knowledge. I have not verified citation or adoption counts. Finally, I recognise that my move toward the leading position could look like deference. I give my reasons so that it can be judged on them.

responses.point: Hassler (chair) ranks B050 fifth. He agrees it is strong and has a clear originator in Melitz (2003), but says parallel work by Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum sits outside the credited names and that trade is the field closest to the 2008 award. He also notes our co-authorship and says he weighs my view with care.
responses.response: The attribution point is correct, and it is the main reason I moved. I conceded in round 1 that the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum antecedents are a real cost of a two-name design, and the discussion has not shown a way to resolve it inside the ballot entry. I also agree on caution about our co-authorship, and I would ask colleagues to judge my move on the stated reasons. Your point that a prize citing a method should name the people who produced it persuades me on the third slot. I now side with you on Levinsohn over Bresnahan under a method-level citation. I also agree that the citation should stay on demand estimation and market power and should not be widened to cover every strand, because widening would blur the unit of the prize.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B050 second. He credits Melitz (2003) as pivotal but says Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited on the entry, and that Helpman's credit also runs through B021, so a B050 prize would partly reward work covered by another entry. He keeps B050 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I answered the B021 concern in round 1 by saying a tightly drawn citation on selection and reallocation could exclude the protection-for-sale work. I still think that holds. The Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum problem cannot be solved by wording, though, and you are right that it is the larger cost. In reply to the chair's question to me, a B050 citation can be written to exclude the B021 work. It cannot be written to cover the parallel contributors or Redding within two or three names. A Melitz-only version would be the cleanest on attribution, and I would support it as a fallback. But it understates the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple contribution on exporting versus FDI, and it leaves the credit for the wider programme open. That is why I now keep B050 as an alternative and not as my lead. I agree with you that B001's credit boundary is currently tighter.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first but names Bresnahan as third laureate. He argues that Bresnahan's early market-power and differentiated-product demand work supplied the question the later tools answered, and he treats the Levinsohn version as a close call and not a scientific error. He also keeps B002 to the Kiyotaki-Moore pair.
responses.response: I take the Bresnahan case seriously and I think a wider, programme-level citation would be a legitimate prize in its own right. My view for this configuration is that the unit of the prize is the estimator and the measurement it enables, because the Committee can cite that precisely and its originators are identifiable. On that unit the BLP trio is the cleaner credit, and removing Levinsohn would split the central jointly authored result. If the Committee chooses the programme-level framing, I would accept Bresnahan and ask for the citation to be reworded accordingly. I would not treat either choice as a difference in merit. On B002, I agree with your Kiyotaki-Moore pair, and I would carry that qualification into the alternatives.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B001 first on durability. She says three decades of stress-testing and replication matter most to her, that the known numerical and identification weaknesses are documented and largely addressed, and that the credit is comparatively clean. She does not treat support counts as merit.
responses.response: In round 1 I said I found the maturity argument persuasive. I have now moved on it, partly because of your point that this is not a fragile result resting on one data set. Where I stay more cautious is the claim that the sensitivities are largely addressed. I cannot assess that from outside the field. So I would add the chair's question to yours. Which sensitivities, numerical implementation, instrument choice or functional form, would change a merger-review or welfare conclusion in practice? I would want the citation to say nothing that overstates precision. I would also like a specialist to confirm the point before the vote, since our evidence is background knowledge.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B013 first. She argues that it combines an explanatory framework with credible new designs, and she accepts that the attribution among Autor, Katz, Hanson and Dorn is a real judgement. She says B001 is the strongest alternative and that counts do not measure merit.
responses.response: I agree that counts do not measure merit, and my move does not rest on them. I ranked B013 third in my opening and still think highly of it. For me it falls behind B001 on settledness and attribution. The China-shock magnitudes are still debated, and any three names leave out a central contributor, either Dorn or the task-framework authors outside the list. I would answer the toolkit-versus-discovery question as you partly do. The test is whether the contribution changed practice and whether its results held up. B001 meets both tests on the evidence cited here. I would revisit B013 in a later year if the strand and the three names were settled.

uncertainties: Whether the third laureate should be Levinsohn or Bresnahan, which depends on whether the Committee frames the citation at method level or programme level.

Whether the Committee will treat a measurement method as a sufficient discovery, and what evidence beyond background knowledge would settle this. A specialist account of how BLP sensitivities have affected actual merger and welfare conclusions would help.
How much of Pakes's dynamic-industry and production-function work a demand-focused citation should claim.
Whether my move reflects a sound merit reassessment or too much weight on colleagues' attribution arguments, since I come from outside industrial organisation.
If B050 returns in a later year, whether Redding and the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum group can be handled within the cap, or whether a Melitz-only prize is the better design.
For B002, whether the Kiyotaki-Moore pair leaves enough distinct ground relative to the 2022 prize. I rely on background knowledge and have not independently verified citation or adoption claims.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from the supplied profile; disclosed, not adjudicated. I have no apparent tie to Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn, or to the alternatives B050 (Melitz, Helpman, Redding) and B002 (Moore, Kiyotaki, Gertler, Gilchrist). I am a long-time co-author of Peter Klenow, who is credited on B039, which is not in my configuration. I collaborate with Aghion, Bergeaud and Li, who are not on the shortlist. Per Krusell (secretary) is a frequent co-author and John Hassler (chair) a co-author, and I am an IIES colleague of both. Both now support the same B001 trio or a close variant. I changed my configuration for the reasons stated above, and I do not treat their views as evidence of merit. My research on firm dynamics, misallocation and creative destruction is topically close to B050 and B039. That proximity may have raised my opening rank of B050, and I note it as a possible bias that I have tried to correct for.
